import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L Empty n

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L ℕ n

abbrev SyntacticFormulaᵢ (L : Language) := SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ L 0

variable {L : Language}

namespace Semiformulaᵢ

instance : Bot (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨falsum⟩

instance : Arrow (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨imp⟩

abbrev neg (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n := φ ➝ ⊥

instance : LogicalConnective (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) where
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  tilde := neg

lemma neg_def (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

instance : Quantifier (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ) where
  univ := all
  ex := ex

section ToString

variable [∀ k, ToString (L.Func k)] [∀ k, ToString (L.Rel k)] [ToString ξ]

def toStr : ∀ {n}, Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → String
  | _, ⊤                         => "\\top"
  | _, ⊥                         => "\\bot"
  | _, rel (arity := 0) r _      => "{" ++ toString r ++ "}"
  | _, rel (arity := _ + 1) r v  => "{" ++ toString r ++ "} \\left(" ++ String.vecToStr (fun i => toString (v i)) ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ⋏ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ⋎ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ➝ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\to "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | n, all φ                     => "(\\forall x_{" ++ toString n ++ "}) " ++ toStr φ
  | n, ex φ                      => "(\\exists x_{" ++ toString n ++ "}) " ++ toStr φ

instance : Repr (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨fun t _ => toStr t⟩

instance : ToString (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨toStr⟩

end ToString

  exact?

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L ℕ n

C0_dependencies.name: LO.FirstOrder.Semiformulaᵢ.toStr
C0_dependencies.content:
def toStr : ∀ {n}, Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → String
  | _, ⊤                         => "\\top"
  | _, ⊥                         => "\\bot"
  | _, rel (arity := 0) r _      => "{" ++ toString r ++ "}"
  | _, rel (arity := _ + 1) r v  => "{" ++ toString r ++ "} \\left(" ++ String.vecToStr (fun i => toString (v i)) ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ⋏ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ⋎ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ➝ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\to "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | n, all φ                     => "(\\forall x_{" ++ toString n ++ "}) " ++ toStr φ
  | n, ex φ                      => "(\\exists x_{" ++ toString n ++ "}) " ++ toStr φ
C0_dependencies.compilationAlias:
def toStr : ∀ {n}, Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → String
  | _, ⊤                         => "\\top"

C0_dependencies.name: LO.FirstOrder.Semiformulaᵢ.toStr
C0_dependencies.content:
def toStr : ∀ {n}, Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → String
  | _, ⊤                         => "\\top"
  | _, ⊥                         => "\\bot"
  | _, rel (arity := 0) r _      => "{" ++ toString r ++ "}"
  | _, rel (arity := _ + 1) r v  => "{" ++ toString r ++ "} \\left(" ++ String.vecToStr (fun i => toString (v i)) ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ⋏ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\land " ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ⋎ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\lor "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | _, φ ➝ ψ                     => "\\left(" ++ toStr φ ++ " \\to "  ++ toStr ψ ++ "\\right)"
  | n, all φ                     => "(\\forall x_{" ++ toString n ++ "}) " ++ toStr φ
  | n, ex φ                      => "(\\exists x_{" ++ toString n ++ "}) " ++ toStr φ

  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

informal_statement: For every natural number $n$, there exists a prime number $p$ such that $p > n$. This implies that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
informal_proof:
Let $n$ be any arbitrary natural number.

1. Consider the number $m = (n+1)! + 1$, where $(n+1)!$ denotes the factorial of $(n+1)$.
2. Note that $m$ is greater than 1 because factorials are always greater than 1 for positive integers.
3. By the lemma `exists_prime_factor`, which states that every integer greater than 1 has at least one prime factor, there exists a prime number $p$ that divides $m$.
4. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that $p \leq n$. This implies that $p$ is one of the factors in the factorial $(n+1)!$.
5. Since $p$ divides $(n+1)!$, it also divides $m - (n+1)! = 1$.
6. However, a prime number cannot divide 1, as the only divisor of 1 is itself, and primes are defined to be greater than 1.
7. This contradiction suggests our initial assumption $p \leq n$ must be false.
8. Therefore, $p > n$.
9. Since $n$ was an arbitrary natural number, this completes the proof that for every natural number $n$, there exists a prime number $p$ such that $p > n$.
10. Thus, there can exist no finite set of primes, as for any finite set, there would be a larger prime number not contained within it.
11. Hence, there are infinitely many prime numbers.

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L Empty n

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L ℕ n

abbrev SyntacticFormulaᵢ (L : Language) := SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ L 0

variable {L : Language}

namespace Semiformulaᵢ

instance : Bot (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨falsum⟩

instance : Arrow (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨imp⟩

abbrev neg (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n := φ ➝ ⊥

instance : LogicalConnective (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) where
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  tilde := neg

lemma neg_def (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := by exact?

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L Empty n

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L ℕ n

abbrev SyntacticFormulaᵢ (L : Language) := SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ L 0

variable {L : Language}

namespace Semiformulaᵢ

instance : Bot (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨falsum⟩

instance : Arrow (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨imp⟩

abbrev neg (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n := φ ➝ ⊥

instance : LogicalConnective (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) where
  wedge := and
  vee := or
  top := verum
  tilde := neg

lemma neg_def (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl
annotation: lemma neg_def (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : ∼φ = φ ➝ ⊥ := rfl

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: For any two formulas φ and ψ at a given level k, if their "exItr" (existing iteration) at level k are equal, then the original formulas φ and ψ must also be equal. This establishes that the "exItr" function is injective at each level k.
informal_proof:
We will prove this statement using mathematical induction on the level k.

**Base Case (k = 0):**  
At level 0, let's consider the simplest case where the "exItr" function is applied. By definition, we assume that "exItr_0(φ)" equals "exItr_0(ψ)". According to the properties of the "exItr" function, this equality implies that φ itself equals ψ. Thus, the base case holds.

**Inductive Step:**  
Assume that for some arbitrary level k, if "exItr_k(φ)" equals "exItr_k(ψ)", then φ equals ψ. We need to show that the same holds for the next level, k+1.

By the inductive hypothesis, we know that if "exItr_k(φ)" equals "exItr_k(ψ)", then φ must equal ψ. Now, applying the "exItr_succ" lemma, which defines the successor case for the "exItr" function, we see that the structure of formulas at level k+1 builds upon those at level k. Since the "exItr" function uniquely identifies formulas at each level based on the inductive hypothesis, it follows that "exItr_{k+1}(φ)" equals "exItr_{k+1}(ψ)" only if φ equals ψ.

Therefore, by induction, the "exItr" function is injective at every level k, proving that if "exItr^k(φ)" equals "exItr^k(ψ)", then φ must equal ψ.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.

  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

informal_statement: For any language \( L \) and context \( \xi \), and for any formula \( \varphi \) within \( L \) under context \( \xi \) with \( k \) universally quantified variables, the statement \( \forall^{\,k} \varphi \) is equivalent to another such formula \( \psi \), implies that \( \varphi \) itself is identical to \( \psi \).
informal_proof:
To establish this, we proceed by induction on the number of universally quantified variables \( k \).

**Base Case** (\( k = 0 \)):
When \( k = 0 \), there are no universally quantified variables, and the statement \( \forall^{\,0} \varphi \) reduces to the formula \( \varphi \) itself. If \( \forall^{\,0} \varphi \equiv \forall^{\,0} \psi \), then \( \varphi \equiv \psi \) trivially.

**Inductive Step**:
Assume that for some \( k \), if two \( k \)-universally-quantified formulas are equivalent, then they are identical. Now consider \( k + 1 \). If \( \forall^{\,k+1} \varphi \equiv \forall^{\,k+1} \psi \), then by the definition of universal quantification, the quantified formulas are equivalent for all assignments of the \( k + 1 \) variables. Using the induction hypothesis on the \( k \) variables, we can infer that the remaining parts of the formulas (now \( k \)-universally-quantified) are identical. This leads to the conclusion that the entire formulas \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \) must be identical.

Thus, by induction, the equivalence of two universally quantified formulas with the same number of universally quantified variables implies their identity.

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L Empty n

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L ℕ n

abbrev SyntacticFormulaᵢ (L : Language) := SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ L 0

variable {L : Language}

namespace Semiformulaᵢ

instance : Bot (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨falsum⟩

instance : Arrow (Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) := ⟨imp⟩

abbrev neg (φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n) : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n := by exact?

informal_statement: The existence closure operation is injective; that is, if the existence closure of two formulas φ and ψ are equivalent, then the original formulas φ and ψ must themselves be identical.
informal_proof:
To establish that the existence closure operation is injective, we consider two formulas φ and ψ and their respective existence closures. The key idea is to demonstrate that if the existence closure of φ is equivalent to the existence closure of ψ, then φ and ψ must be the same formula.

We approach this by induction on the structure of the formulas (parallel to the formal proof's induction on n). The base case corresponds to the simplest formulas, typically atomic statements or variables. In this base case, the existence closure operation directly yields the original formula, ensuring their equivalence implies their identical nature.

For the inductive step, we assume that the property holds for formulas of a certain complexity and show it extends to formulas with an additional layer of complexity (e.g., involving logical connectives or quantifiers). By applying the induction hypothesis, we decompose the existence closure of the complex formula into components, each of which inherits the property from the inductive hypothesis.

By systematically applying these steps, we confirm that the existence closure operation preserves the identity of the original formula, thereby proving its injectivity.

informal_statement: The univalence closure of two semiformulas is injective if and only if the semiformulas themselves are identical.
informal_proof:
To establish the injectivity of the univalence closure for semiformulas, we proceed by induction on the structure of the semiformulas.

**Base Case:**  
Consider the simplest semiformulas, which typically correspond to propositional variables or atomic statements. Suppose we have two identical atomic statements, φ and ψ. Clearly, their univalence closures will be identical, as there is no distinction between φ and ψ.

**Inductive Step:**  
Assume that for any two semiformulas of a given complexity level, if their univalence closures are identical, then the semiformulas themselves are identical. Now, consider two semiformulas φ and ψ that are built from their sub-semiformulas using logical connectives or quantifiers.

By the inductive hypothesis, if the closures of their respective sub-semiformulas are identical, then the sub-semiformulas themselves must be identical. Extending this to the entire formulas by applying the univalence closure operation, we maintain equality throughout the construction of the formulas.

Thus, by induction, the univalence closure of any two semiformulas is injective precisely when the semiformulas themselves are identical.

<STATEMENT>
If the existence of φ is equal to the existence of ψ, then φ must be equivalent to ψ.
</STATEMENT>

<PROOF>
To understand why the equivalence of existence claims implies the equivalence of the contained statements, let's break it down.

1. **Understanding Equality of Existence Claims**: The expression ∃' φ represents "there exists at least one case where φ is true." Similarly, ∃' ψ represents "there exists at least one case where ψ is true." If these are equal, it means that the conditions for φ being true and ψ being true are essentially the same.

2. **Implications of Equal Existence**: If every time φ is true, ψ is also true, and every time ψ is true, φ is also true, then the two statements must inherently convey the same meaning. This mutual implication creates an equivalence between φ and ψ.

3. **Introduction of Logical Equivalence**: The equivalence between existence claims implies a bi-conditional relationship—whenever one is true, the other must be as well, and vice versa. This mutual condition can only hold true if the contained statements φ and ψ are themselves equivalent.

4. **Conclusion of Equivalence**: Therefore, if ∃' φ equals ∃' ψ, it logically follows that φ must be equivalent to ψ. This ensures that both statements are interchangeable in any logical context without altering the truth value of the existence claims.

This step-by-step reasoning demonstrates that the initial implication of equivalent existence leads inevitably to the equivalence of the contained statements.

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L Empty n

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L ℕ n

abbrev SyntacticFormulaᵢ (L : Language) := by exact?

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := Semiformulaᵢ L Empty n

abbrev SyntacticSemiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := by exact?

<STATEMENT>

For all formulas φ₁, φ₂, ψ₁, and ψ₂, if φ₁ → φ₂ is equivalent to ψ₁ → ψ₂, then φ₁ is equivalent to ψ₁ and φ₂ is equivalent to ψ₂.

</STATEMENT>
<PROOF>

By the properties of implication in classical logic, specifically the structure of implication as defined by the `Arrow.arrow` lemma, if φ₁ → φ₂ is equal to ψ₁ → ψ₂, then the antecedents and consequents of these implications must individually be equal. This is because the form of an implication dictates the relationship between its antecedent and consequent. Therefore, φ₁ must equal ψ₁ and φ₂ must equal ψ₂.

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | imp    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

abbrev Formulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) := Semiformulaᵢ L ξ 0

abbrev Sentenceᵢ (L : Language) := Formulaᵢ L Empty

abbrev Semisentenceᵢ (L : Language) (n : ℕ) := by exact?

informal_statement: For any semiformulas φ₁, φ₂, ψ₁, and ψ₂, the equivalence of their combined forms using the operation `⋎` implies the individual equivalence of each pair φ₁ = ψ₁ and φ₂ = ψ₂. In other words, the operation `⋎` ensures that only identical constituent semiformulas produce identical combined forms.
informal_proof: To establish this, suppose that the combined form of φ₁ and φ₂ using the operation `⋎` is identical to the combined form of ψ₁ and ψ₂, i.e., φ₁ ⋎ φ₂ = ψ₁ ⋎ ψ₂. By the definition of `⋎`, this equality holds if and only if both φ₁ and φ₂ exactly match ψ₁ and ψ₂, respectively. Therefore, it must be that φ₁ = ψ₁ and φ₂ = ψ₂. This demonstrates that `⋎` uniquely determines the equivalence of its components, confirming the lemma.

informal_statement: For any four statements φ₁, ψ₁, φ₂, and ψ₂, if the conjunction (φ₁ ∧ φ₂) is equivalent to (ψ₁ ∧ ψ₂), then φ₁ must be equivalent to ψ₁ and φ₂ must be equivalent to ψ₂. This property is known as the injectivity of the conjunction operation.
informal_proof:
Assume that (φ₁ ∧ φ₂) ≡ (ψ₁ ∧ ψ₂).

1. By the properties of logical conjunction, specifically its injectivity, if the conjunction of two statements is equivalent, then each corresponding statement must be equivalent.
   
2. Therefore, φ₁ must be equivalent to ψ₁, and φ₂ must be equivalent to ψ₂.

3. This follows because if there were any difference between φ₁ and ψ₁ or between φ₂ and ψ₂, their conjunctions would not be equivalent.

Hence, we conclude that if (φ₁ ∧ φ₂) ≡ (ψ₁ ∧ ψ₂), then φ₁ ≡ ψ₁ and φ₂ ≡ ψ₂.

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

namespace LO.FirstOrder

inductive Semiformulaᵢ (L : Language) (ξ : Type*) : ℕ → Type _ where
  | verum  {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | falsum {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | rel    {n} : {arity : ℕ} → L.Rel arity → (Fin arity → Semiterm L ξ n) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | and    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | or     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

  | all    {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n
  | ex     {n} : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ (n + 1) → Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

informal_statement: The negation of a formula φ, denoted as neg φ, is defined as φ implying a contradiction (typically symbolized as ⊥).
informal_proof:
To understand why this definition of negation works, consider the following reasoning:

1. **Assumption**: Let's start by assuming φ is a formula that represents a proposition.
2. **Definition**: The negation of φ, written as neg φ, is defined as φ → ⊥, where ⊥ represents a contradiction or a statement that is always false.
3. **Implication**: In logic, an implication φ → ψ is only false when φ is true and ψ is false. 
4. **Application to Negation**:
    - If φ is true, then according to our definition, neg φ would be true only if φ → ⊥ is true. But since φ is true and ⊥ is false, φ → ⊥ would be false, making neg φ false.
    - Conversely, if φ is false, then φ → ⊥ would be true because an implication with a false antecedent is always true, making neg φ true.
5. **Equivalence**:
    - When we say φ implies a contradiction, we are asserting that assuming φ leads to an impossible situation. Therefore, ¬φ must hold to prevent this contradiction.
    - This aligns with the classical logic principle that ¬φ (not φ) is true exactly when φ is false.
6. **Conclusion**: By defining neg φ as φ → ⊥, we effectively capture the essence of negation in classical logic, where a statement and its negation cannot both be true, and one of them must always hold.

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

For any language \( L \) and any natural number \( n \), there is a one-to-one correspondence between syntactic semi-formulas in \( L \) with \( n \) variables and formal proofs in \( L \) with \( n \) variables, where each semi-formula corresponds to exactly one formal proof.

<PROOF>

To establish the correspondence between syntactic semi-formulas and formal proofs in the language \( L \) with \( n \) variables, we proceed as follows:

1. **Definition of Semi-Formulas**: Begin by defining syntactic semi-formulas in \( L \) with \( n \) variables. These include propositional variables, logical connectives, and quantifiers, combining according to the syntax rules of \( L \).
   
2. **Truth Definition**: Utilize Tarski’s truth definition to associate each semi-formula with a condition on the \( n \) variables, thereby establishing a relationship between the structure of the semi-formula and its semantic interpretation.

3. **Bijection Construction**: Construct a bijection between syntactic semi-formulas and formal proofs by deeming a semi-formula to correspond to the formal proof of its own truth condition. This ensures that each semi-formula is paired uniquely with its corresponding proof.

4. **Inductive Correspondence**: Extend the correspondence inductively to formulas of increasing complexity. Assume the correspondence holds for simpler formulas and show it continues to hold as more complex formulas are built up from these simpler ones.

5. **Proof Verification**: Confirm that the bijection preserves the equivalence of statements by verifying that statements are equivalent if and only if their corresponding proofs are identical. This ensures that the semantic and syntactic aspects align perfectly.

6. **Conclusion**: With the bijection established and its properties verified, conclude that there is indeed a one-to-one correspondence between syntactic semi-formulas and formal proofs in \( L \) with \( n \) variables.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

import Foundation.FirstOrder.Basic

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

This file defines the formulas of first-order logic.

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

/-!
# Formulas of intuitionistic first-order logic

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

`φ : Semiformulaᵢ L ξ n` is a (semi-)formula of language `L` with bounded variables of `Fin n` and free variables of `ξ`.
The quantification is represented by de Bruijn index.

-/

informal_statement: For any propositions \( a \) and \( b \), \( a \lor b \) is equivalent to \( b \lor a \).
informal_proof:
To prove that \( a \lor b \) is equivalent to \( b \lor a \), we proceed as follows: For an arbitrary pair of propositions \( a \) and \( b \), we consider the two possible cases of the disjunction \( a \lor b \). 

1. If \( a \) is true, then \( b \lor a \) is also true because \( a \) is part of the disjunction.
2. If \( b \) is true, then \( a \lor b \) is equivalent to \( b \lor a \), which is trivially true.

Since both cases hold, \( a \lor b \) implies \( b \lor a \). Similarly, by symmetry, if \( b \lor a \) is true, then \( a \lor b \) must also be true. Therefore, \( a \lor b \) is indeed equivalent to \( b \lor a \).

informal_statement: For all natural numbers \( n \), if \( \varphi \) is a semiformula in \( n+1 \) variables, then \( \varphi \) is also a semiformula in \( n \) variables.
informal_proof:

informal_statement: For a given natural number \( n \), denoting the arity, and a relation of that arity, there exists a semiformula constructed from terms defined for each argument position within the language \( L \), indexed by a variable \( \xi \).
informal_proof:
First, let's fix a natural number \( n \), which represents the number of arguments (arity) for our relation. This means we have \( n \) argument positions that the relation can take.

For each index \( i \) within the finite set \( \text{Fin } n \), which denotes the set of indices from 0 to \( n - 1 \), we can define a term \( t_i \) in the language \( L \) using the variable \( \xi \). Since these indices specify the positions of the arguments, each \( t_i \) corresponds to the term in the \( i \)-th argument position of our relation.

Given that \( t_i \) is a well-formed term in the language \( L \) for each \( i \), and considering that the language \( L \) includes the necessary symbols and structure to express such terms, each \( t_i \) can be combined to form a semiformula \( \phi \) in the context of the language \( L \) with the variable \( \xi \).

Specifically, since \( \text{Semiformulaᵢ } L \xi n \) denotes the set of semiformulas in language \( L \) with \( n \) arguments indexed by \( \xi \), the semiformula \( \phi \) can be constructed by appropriately combining the terms \( t_i \) for each \( i \) in \( \text{Fin } n \).

Therefore, by the way terms are combined in the language \( L \) and the definition of a semiformula, we can confirm that there exists a term \( t_i \) in \( L \xi n \) for each \( i \) in \( \text{Fin } n \), and these terms together form a valid semiformula \( \phi \) in \( \text{Semiformulaᵢ } L \xi n \).

This completes the informal proof, demonstrating that for each argument position, there exists a term in the language that can be combined into a semiformula as required.
